messages.subject: New features: more flexible priorities and seizes
messages.subject_clean: New features: more flexible priorities and seizes
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Until now, the prioritization values (priority, preemptible, restart) were assigned to seize activities, and they were static values, so it was not possible to change them dynamically through a function, as Cameron was trying to do in this thread <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/simmer-devel/Avssvd6loHo/1DEtg5m7AAAJ>.

Now, I’ve moved the prioritization definition to add_generator, which has several advantages:
Symmetry with add_resource, which defines resource preemptiveness.
Simpler syntax for seize.
More natural interpretation of prioritization values as attributes of arrivals from the same generator, rather than attributes of a seize.
More flexibility, since there is a new activity called set_prioritization, which accepts a custom function as well as static parameters, to change these values dynamically inside the trajectory.

See #69 <https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer/issues/69#issuecomment-230149192> for more information and working examples.

Many models require an arrival to do something if it gets rejected when trying to seize a resource. Some time ago, I had proposed a new activity called ifseize to cover this requirement. As #69 alleviates seize‘s syntax, I’ve finally decided to add this feature to seize itself (and seize_selected).

The implementation and general operation have a lot in common with a branch. In this case, you can define two optional subtrajectories:
post.seize: if present, it’s executed after a successful seize. As in a branch, a flag continue controls whether the arrival must continue in the main trajectory or not.
reject: if present, it’s executed after an unsuccessful seize (a rejection). Instead of getting dropped, the arrival follows this subtrajectory and, again, a flag continue controls whether the subtrajectory must be linked to the main trajectory.

See #49 <https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer/issues/49#issuecomment-230466052> for more information and working examples.

Finally, I’d like to share some numbers with you. I’m proud that we have reached 50 closed issues on GitHub, 19 of them since this mailing list was created. This list has proved to be a great source of feedback. So thank you all, and spread the word of simmer. ;-)

Regards,
​
--
Iñaki Úcar
http://www.enchufa2.es
@Enchufa2 <https://twitter.com/#%21/Enchufa2>

Hi Iñaki

Could I use this or something similar to leave a branch without leaving the whole trajectory? Am modelling a process that has two branches, the first time it should always go for the first one but then, with some probability related decision, it should leave and take the other branch. I have this up to now but it is not working:

LHD <- create_trajectory("Process") %>%
     set_attribute("Carga1", 0) %>%
     set_attribute("Carga1.2", 0) %>%
    set_attribute("HangUp",0) %>%
    set_attribute("Camino",1) %>%  # The first time will always go for the first path.

     branch(function(attrs) ifelse(attrs[["Camino"]]==1,1,2),c(T,T),
         create_trajectory("Branch1") %>%

         set_attribute("Carga1", function(attrs) attrs[["Carga1"]] + rnorm(1,19)) %>%
         seize("Drawpoint1",1)   %>%
         timeout(function() rnorm(1,2)) %>%
         release("Drawpoint1",1) %>%
         seize("CamEx1",1)   %>%
         timeout(function() rnorm(1,10)) %>%
         release("CamEx1",1) %>%
         seize("Chanc",1)   %>%
         timeout(function() rnorm(1,5)) %>%
         release("Chanc",1)  %>%
         seize("CamEx1",1)   %>%
         timeout(function() rnorm(1,10)) %>%
         release("CamEx1",1) %>%
        set_attribute("HangUp", function(attrs) rnorm(1,10)) %>%
        branch(function(attrs) ifelse(attrs[["HangUp"]]<9,1,2),c(T,T), # If HangUp is smaller than 9, then it should change the attribute "Camino" and then go back to the first branch and take the other path. Otherwise it only loses some time and goes back to the line where attribute "Carga1" is modified.

             create_trajectory("Alt1") %>%
                 set_attribute("Camino",2) %>%
                 rollback(amount=15,times=2),
             create_trajectory("Alt2") %>%
                 timeout(0.1)
             ) %>%
         rollback(amount=15, check=function(attrs) attrs[["Carga1"]] < 900),

         ........................

Currently my code is not doing what I want and am struggling to find a solution. Any advice would by appreciated.

Thanks a lot in advance.

Juan

Hi Juan, welcome to this list.

leave doesn’t help here. It does what it promises: the arrival leaves, is dropped. Instead, you only need to increment the first rollback to amount=17, and it will point to the first branch, so your problem is solved.

To debug these questions, you can print the trajectory, and you’ll see which activity the rollback is pointing to. For instance, let’s take the following trajectory. I’m going to change the amount to rollback (1, 2, 3) and print the trajectory. Note the last line of each print:
t <- create_trajectory() %>%
  seize("dummy", 1) %>%
  branch(function() 1, T,
         create_trajectory() %>%
           timeout(1) %>%
           rollback(amount=1, 1))
t
#> simmer trajectory: anonymous, 4 activities
#> { Activity: Seize        | resource: dummy | amount: 1 }
#> { Activity: Branch       | option: 0x44b1468 }
#>   Fork 1, continue,  simmer trajectory: anonymous, 2 activities
#>   { Activity: Timeout      | delay: 1 }
#>   { Activity: Rollback     | amount: 1 (Timeout), times: 1 }
t <- create_trajectory() %>%
  seize("dummy", 1) %>%
  branch(function() 1, T,
         create_trajectory() %>%
           timeout(1) %>%
           rollback(amount=2, 1))
t
#> simmer trajectory: anonymous, 4 activities
#> { Activity: Seize        | resource: dummy | amount: 1 }
#> { Activity: Branch       | option: 0x3ce6c58 }
#>   Fork 1, continue,  simmer trajectory: anonymous, 2 activities
#>   { Activity: Timeout      | delay: 1 }
#>   { Activity: Rollback     | amount: 2 (Branch), times: 1 }
t <- create_trajectory() %>%
  seize("dummy", 1) %>%
  branch(function() 1, T,
         create_trajectory() %>%
           timeout(1) %>%
           rollback(amount=3, 1))
t
#> simmer trajectory: anonymous, 4 activities

#> { Activity: Branch       | option: 0x4702610 }
#>   Fork 1, continue,  simmer trajectory: anonymous, 2 activities

messages.subject: New feature: clone & synchronize
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Our repertoire includes two new activities: clone and synchronize. The first one is a kind of parallel branch: it clones the arrival and processes each copy in parallel through user-defined sub-trajectories. Then, you can synchronize them, i.e., merge all those threads again into a single one.

See #71 <https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer/issues/71> for more details. The "Advanced Trajectory Usage" <https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer/blob/master/vignettes/C-trajectories.Rmd> vignette has been updated with this and other examples. And as always, check out the master branch if you wish to test it.

Regards,
--
